summary: Defines a framework for applying security services to MIME body parts, with multipart/signed for digital signatures and multipart/encrypted for encryption. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1847 defines two MIME structures for carrying signed or encrypted message parts. It specifies where the protected content and control information go, but separate documents must define how signing or encryption works.

questions: how do mime security multiparts work
why must signed mime be 7 bit
subtitle: A MIME framework for carrying signed or encrypted body parts with their control information.

tldr.problem: MIME defines message-body structure but does not itself provide security protection for its content.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted. Each contains exactly two body parts, and a protocol parameter identifies the separate security protocol and control information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1847 is a Proposed Standard framework; it does not define a particular signature or encryption mechanism.

today: RFC 1847 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC defines a framework, not a particular signature or encryption protocol.

sections.title: A Security Framework for MIME
sections.content:
MIME defines how Internet mail bodies can contain structured text and non-text content. The basic MIME specification does not provide specific security protection.

RFC 1847 defines a framework for using security protocols with MIME. A mail application needs both this framework and a separate protocol that defines the security processing.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME can describe many kinds of message content but does not protect that content by itself. This RFC gives other security protocols a standard place in a MIME message.

sections.title: Two Security Multipart Types
sections.content:
The framework defines two multipart subtypes. multipart/signed supports authentication and integrity, with control information in the second part. multipart/encrypted supports confidentiality, with control information in the first part.

Both contain exactly two related body parts and require a protocol parameter. That parameter identifies the control-information type and determines which separate protocol processes it.
sections.plainLanguage: Both types have two body parts, but they put the protected content and control information in different positions. The protocol parameter tells the application how to handle the control information.

sections.title: The multipart/signed Format
sections.content:
The signed subtype requires boundary, protocol, and micalg parameters. The first part is the signed MIME body part, including its MIME headers. The second contains information needed to verify the signature.

The micalg parameter names the message integrity check algorithm. If the object may pass through standard Internet SMTP, the signed body is limited to 7-bit data; 8-bit or binary content must be encoded as quoted-printable or base64.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part contains the signed content, and the second part contains verification information. Mail systems must not alter the signed content while it travels.

sections.title: Creating and Verifying a Signed Part
sections.content:
To create a signed part, the application prepares the content and MIME headers, applies the security protocol's signing preparation, and obtains both the protected body and control information. The MIME agent places these in the first and second parts.

To verify, the receiving agent passes the first part and control information to the protocol's verification process. It makes the result available to the user and continues with the body part returned by that process.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender prepares the MIME part and obtains a signature and its control information. The receiver gives both parts to the matching verification process and reports its result.

sections.title: The multipart/encrypted Format
sections.content:
The encrypted subtype requires boundary and protocol parameters. Its first part contains the information needed to decrypt; its second part contains encrypted data labeled application/octet-stream.

The encrypted data includes the original MIME headers, so its type cannot be determined from the outer headers alone. A receiving application should wait until decryption completes before trying to display the content.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part gives the decryption protocol's control information, and the second contains encrypted data. The receiver must decrypt before it can interpret the original content.

sections.title: Protocol and Key-Management Requirements
sections.content:
A minimal MIME application can identify the protected-data and control-information parts. Complete support also requires recognizing the protocol parameter and applying the processing defined for that value.

The separate security-protocol specification must define the parameter value, required processing, and exact control-information format. It must also explain how cryptographic material, such as a signer's public key, is distributed.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework identifies where security information goes, but not how that information works. Each security protocol must define its processing and how a receiver obtains the needed keys.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes an enhancement to MIME for signed and encrypted body parts. For multipart/signed, intermediaries must treat the complete container as opaque and must not alter it during transit.

Actual signing, encryption, and key handling depend on the protocol selected by the protocol parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework supports security but does not supply the security algorithm. Mail systems must not change a signed container while it travels.
